newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Australia's Howard praises economic ties with China.
newsitem.headline: Australia's Howard praises economic ties with China.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard said on Friday economic relations between Australia and China were in good shape, but Canberra will not shy away from raising concerns over human rights with its neighbours.
"Australia and China have a lot in common for the future," Howard told reporters before leaving for China after a brief visit to Singapore. "We have a good economic relationship."
He said Australia had to be sensible in raising human rights issues with countries such as China by not lecturing.
"It's never possible that human rights issues won't come up in a bilateral relationship," he said. "(But) one shouldn't be overly hectoring or moralising."
Sino-Australian relations soured soon after Howard's Liberal Party took power after defeating the long-ruling Labour Party in the March 1996 Australian elections.
Beijing denounced a visit last September to Australia by Tibet's spiritual leader, the Dalai Lama, whom China accuses of separatist ambitions for his homeland.

Last August, China also accused Australia of moving too close to the United States after U.S. Secretary of Defence William Perry described Japan and Australia as the northern and southern anchors of Washington's Asian security arrangements.
Howard dismissed the criticism about Australia's defence links with Washington.
"It is not directed at anybody," he declared. "It is the result of a hard-headed Australian assessment of Australia's national interest."
Australia's relations with Indonesia has also been affected in the past because of Canberra's concerns over human rights.
China is Australia's fifth largest trading partner, with two-way trade reaching US$6.3 billion in the year to June 30, 1996. Howard will return to Australia from China on April 2.
